question:
During shoulder arthroscopy in a 40-year-old female recreational golfer, the articular side of the rotator
cuff is found to be intact. However, after performing a bursectomy in the subacromial space, a
bursal-sided tear measuring 1.5 cm in length (anterior to posterior) and 4 mm in depth from the tendon
surface is discovered, along with surrounding cuff softening. What is the most appropriate course of
action? Answer Choices: (A) Local corticosteroid injection with supervised rehabilitation (B) Consider it
incidental, as this is a common finding in this age group (C) Mini-open repair with side-to-side sutures
(D) Conservative management with physical therapy and activity modification (E) Platelet-rich plasma
injection followed by rehabilitation (F) Debridement with biceps tenotomy (G) Debride the tear and
perform an acromioplasty (H) Subacromial decompression without tear repair (I) Arthroscopic repair of
the bursal-sided tear without conversion (J) Convert it to a full-thickness tear and repair it with suture
anchors
 A. Arthroscopic repair of the bursal-sided tear without conversion
B. Consider it incidental, as this is a common finding in this age group
C. Subacromial decompression without tear repair
D. Debridement with biceps tenotomy
E. Debride the tear and perform an acromioplasty
F. Conservative management with physical therapy and activity modification
G. Platelet-rich plasma injection followed by rehabilitation
H. Local corticosteroid injection with supervised rehabilitation
I. Convert it to a full-thickness tear and repair it with suture anchors
J. Mini-open repair with side-to-side sutures
